items.title: CVE-2026-97644 - Groundhogg <= 4.9 - Authenticated (Sales Person+) Privilege Escalation via Contact Identity Rebinding leading to Administrator Account Takeover to 'user_id' Parameter (v3 /contacts) chained with v4 /emails/test
items.one_liner: Groundhogg plugin up to version 4.9 suffers from an authenticated privilege escalation vulnerability leading to admin takeover.
items.summary: CVE-2026-97644 is a privilege escalation vulnerability in the Groundhogg CRM plugin for WordPress affecting versions up to 4.9. The flaw exists because the `create_contact` function in the v3 REST endpoint fails to enforce ownership guards when passing the security-bearing `user_id` column into the database upsert path. Authenticated attackers with Sales Representative privileges can rebind their contact record to an administrator user ID and chain this with the v4 email-test endpoint to generate an auto-login URL. Consuming this link allows the attacker to call `wp_set_auth_cookie()` and achieve full administrator account takeover.
items.bottom_line: Sales Representative accounts on WordPress sites running Groundhogg <= 4.9 can escalate privileges to full Administrator.

items.one_liner: Photo Reviews for WooCommerce <= 1.2.30 allows unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary site posts.
items.summary: CVE-2026-101923 is a missing authorization vulnerability in the Photo Reviews for WooCommerce plugin for WordPress for versions up to 1.2.30. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to supply arbitrary post IDs via the wcpr_image_upload_id parameter during public review submissions, which are stored without ownership verification in comment meta. When an administrator subsequently deletes the review or when WordPress cron empties the trash, the plugin's deletion handler executes wp_delete_post() on the stored IDs. This results in the permanent deletion of arbitrary posts, pages, products, or media attachments on the site.

items.title: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.
items.one_liner: A new benchmark from Microsoft and Hugging Face shows that nearly 78% of failed agent trials still report clean tool execution while leaving incorrect database states behind.
items.summary: Microsoft and Hugging Face researchers introduced ThinkingBox, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents by grading their terminal backend state and side effects rather than just looking at final responses or tool calls. In a common-set ablation of 121,680 trials across 12 LLM models, researchers found that 79,853 attempts failed executable backend checks, with 67.24% of those failures still terminating cleanly without a reported tool error. Among those failures, executable checks identified wrong field values in 77.61%, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. The findings demonstrate a massive gap where AI agents can appear successful while leaving incorrect records behind in databases.
items.bottom_line: AI agents frequently report successful tool execution while leaving underlying database records in an incorrect state, requiring backend-state verification rather than proxy metrics.
